The term '''center''' or '''centre''' is used in various contexts in [[abstract algebra]] to denote the set of all those elements that [[commutative operation|commute]] with all other elements.
* The [[center of a group]] ''G'' consists of all those elements ''x'' in ''G'' such that ''xg'' = ''gx'' for all ''g'' in ''G''. This is a [[normal subgroup]] of ''G''.
* The similarly named notion for a [[semigroup]] is defined likewise and it is a subsemigroup.<ref name="KilpKilʹp2000">{{cite book |last1=Kilp |first1=Mati |last2=Knauer |first2=Ulrich |last3=Mikhalev |first3=Aleksandr V. |date=2000 |title=Monoids, Acts and Categories |publisher=Walter de Gruyter |series=De Gruyter Expositions in Mathematics |volume=29 |isbn=978-3-11-015248-7 |page=25 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4gPhmmW-EGcC&pg=PA25}}</ref><ref name="Ljapin1968">{{cite book |last=Ljapin |first=E. S. |translator=A. A. Brown |translator2=J. M. Danskin |translator3=D. Foley |translator4=S. H. Gould |translator5=E. Hewitt |translator6=S. A. Walker |translator7=J. A. Zilber |date=1968 |title=Semigroups |series=Translations of Mathematical Monographs |volume=3 |publisher=American Mathematical Soc. |location=Providence, Rhode Island |isbn=978-0-8218-8641-0 |page=96 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=G8pWKPp4tKwC&pg=PA96}}</ref>
* The [[center (ring theory)|center]] of a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] (or an [[associative algebra]]) ''R'' is the subset of ''R'' consisting of all those elements ''x'' of ''R'' such that ''xr'' = ''rx'' for all ''r'' in ''R''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Durbin |first=John R. |title=Modern Algebra: An Introduction |edition=3rd |date=1993 |publisher=John Wiley and Sons |isbn=0-471-51001-7 |page=118 |quote=The ''center'' of a ring ''R'' is defined to be {''c'' ∈ ''R'': ''cr'' = ''rc'' for every ''r'' ∈ ''R''}.}}, Exercise 22.22</ref> The center is a [[commutative ring|commutative]] [[subring]] of ''R''.
* The [[center of a Lie algebra]] ''L'' consists of all those elements ''x'' in ''L'' such that [''x'',''a''] = 0 for all ''a'' in ''L''. This is an [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] of the Lie algebra ''L''.
